title: SYSK Selects: How Yo-Yos Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the Stuff You Should Know episode on yo-yos. Josh introduces it as a selection and the hosts cover the etymology of "yo," the yo-yo's history from ancient toys and Filipino hunting weapons to Pedro Flores, Donald Duncan, the Duncan company's trademark loss and move to Luck, Wisconsin, and then the physics: linear and angular momentum, gyroscopic stability, moment of inertia, the sleeping and waking of a yo-yo, ball-bearing and clutch designs (Yo-Yo with the Brain, No Jive), and yo-yo trivia including Abbie Hoffman's HUAC appearance, Nixon's yo-yo presentation, and yo-yos in space. The episode closes with a listener mail about a charity compilation for Japan earthquake relief.

segments.title: SYSK Selects introduction and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this Selects episode on yo-yos and the hosts banter about backaches and the 1988 film Harlem Nights, where Eddie Murphy uses the word yo in a 1920s setting.

segments.title: Origins of the word yo and early yo-yo history
segments.summary: The hosts trace the word yo from a fifteenth-century hunting cry and sailors' calls to a post-World War Two usage from Italian quarters of Philadelphia. They note the Filipino origin of the modern yo-yo in the 1920s and older ancestors in ancient China and Greece, plus the Greek, Chinese, and European tied-axle designs.

segments.title: Yo-yo names and Filipino hunting weapon origins
segments.summary: The hosts mention earlier European names such as the lemigrette and bandalore, a painting of a French king with a toy, and Napoleon's use of a yo-yo for stress. They describe the early Philippine yo-yo as a large heavy hunting weapon with spikes.

segments.title: Pedro Flores, Donald Duncan, and the yo-yo trademark
segments.summary: A Filipino immigrant, Pedro Flores, started the first modern yo-yo company in the United States in the 1920s and later sold it to Donald Duncan, who bought the yo-yo name. Competitors later challenged the trademark, and federal courts ruled that yo-yo had become generic. Duncan's company went bankrupt, but the Duncan name was sold and survives.

segments.title: Duncan's Luck, Wisconsin factory and National Yo-Yo Day
segments.summary: Duncan moved to Luck, Wisconsin in the 1940s, which became known as the yo-yo capital of the world. The company made yo-yos from maple wood and sold a large number in 1962. June 6 is National Yo-Yo Day, Donald Duncan's birthday.

segments.title: Physics of yo-yos: momentum, gyroscopic stability, and sleeping
segments.summary: The hosts explain that a Filipino-style yo-yo has linear momentum and angular momentum, which lets it sleep at the bottom of the string. They discuss gyroscopic stability, which keeps a spinning yo-yo stable as it rises and falls, and compare it to footballs and curveballs. Tugging the string rewinds the yo-yo because the loose loop reduces friction.

segments.title: Moment of inertia and yo-yo design changes
segments.summary: The hosts explain moment of inertia as resistance to changes in rotation, which increases when mass is placed further from the axis. This explains the inverted, butterfly-style Duncan yo-yos. They discuss the 1960s addition of outer mass and how the Filipino design advanced yo-yo design.

segments.title: Ball bearing and clutch yo-yos, and yo-yo tricks
segments.summary: The hosts describe the ball-bearing yo-yo, which uses inner and outer races so the yo-yo can sleep longer, and the 1990s Yo-Yo with the Brain, a clutch design developed by Michael Caffrey and preceded by Tom Kuhn's No Jive. They also discuss the hosts' tricks such as walk the dog, cat's cradle, and around the world.

segments.title: Yo-yo trivia: Abbie Hoffman, Nixon, and yo-yos in space
segments.summary: Abbie Hoffman was charged with contempt of Congress after performing yo-yo tricks during a House Un-American Activities Committee session. Nixon was presented with a yo-yo in 1974 and failed to make it work. NASA's Toys in Space project tested a yo-yo in microgravity. The hosts end with a search tip for finding yo-yo news.

segments.title: Listener mail on Japan earthquake charity album and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck reads a listener email from a musician promoting a charity compilation for Japan earthquake and tsunami relief, with thirty-seven tracks available at morehopeforjapan.com. The hosts invite listeners to share feedback and close the episode.
